claim: Clonally transmissible cancers are tumour lineages that are transmitted between individuals via the transfer of living cancer cells.
source: Clonally transmissible cancers are tumour lineages that are transmitted between individuals via the transfer of living cancer cells.
evidence: This is a definitional statement that draws from established scientific knowledge about transmissible cancers.

claim: In marine bivalves, leukaemia-like transmissible cancers, called hemic neoplasia (HN), have demonstrated the ability to infect individuals from different species.
source: In marine bivalves, leukaemia-like transmissible cancers, called hemic neoplasia (HN), have demonstrated the ability to infect individuals from different species.
evidence: This statement references established findings about HN in bivalves, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Whole-genome sequencing was performed in eight warty venus clams that were diagnosed with HN.
source: We performed whole-genome sequencing in eight warty venus clams that were diagnosed with HN, from two sampling points located more than 1000 nautical miles away in the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea Coasts of Spain.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: The two sampling points were located more than 1000 nautical miles away in the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea Coasts of Spain.
source: We performed whole-genome sequencing in eight warty venus clams that were diagnosed with HN, from two sampling points located more than 1000 nautical miles away in the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea Coasts of Spain.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the geographic locations of sampling, supported by the study design.

claim: Mitochondrial genome sequencing analysis from neoplastic animals revealed the coexistence of haplotypes from two different clam species.
source: Mitochondrial genome sequencing analysis from neoplastic animals revealed the coexistence of haplotypes from two different clam species.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the sequencing data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: This leukaemia originated in striped venus clams and later transmitted to clams of the species warty venus.
source: Phylogenies estimated from mitochondrial and nuclear markers confirmed this leukaemia originated in striped venus clams and later transmitted to clams of the species warty venus, in which it survives as a contagious cancer.
evidence: This conclusion is based on phylogenetic analysis of mitochondrial and nuclear markers.

claim: The leukaemia survives as a contagious cancer in warty venus clams.
source: Phylogenies estimated from mitochondrial and nuclear markers confirmed this leukaemia originated in striped venus clams and later transmitted to clams of the species warty venus, in which it survives as a contagious cancer.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic data and the presence of the cancer in warty venus specimens.

claim: All studied tumours belong to a single neoplastic lineage that spreads in the Seas of Southern Europe.
source: The analysis of mitochondrial and nuclear gene sequences supports all studied tumours belong to a single neoplastic lineage that spreads in the Seas of Southern Europe.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the analysis of mitochondrial and nuclear gene sequences showing no nucleotide diversity.

claim: Cancers are clonal cell lineages that arise due to somatic changes that promote cell proliferation and survival.
source: Cancers are clonal cell lineages that arise due to somatic changes that promote cell proliferation and survival (Stratton et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a general statement about cancer biology supported by a citation.

claim: Natural selection operating on cancers favours the outgrowth of malignant clones with replicative immortality.
source: Although natural selection operating on cancers favours the outgrowth of malignant clones with replicative immortality, the continued survival of a cancer is generally restricted by the lifespan of its host.
evidence: This is a statement about cancer evolution based on established knowledge.

claim: The continued survival of a cancer is generally restricted by the lifespan of its host.
source: Although natural selection operating on cancers favours the outgrowth of malignant clones with replicative immortality, the continued survival of a cancer is generally restricted by the lifespan of its host.
evidence: This is a general principle about cancer biology.

claim: Clonally transmissible cancers can survive beyond the death of their hosts.
source: However, clonally transmissible cancers – from now on, transmissible cancers – are somatic cell lineages that are transmitted between individuals via the transfer of living cancer cells, meaning that they can survive beyond the death of their hosts (Murchison, 2008).
evidence: This is a defining characteristic of transmissible cancers, supported by citation.

claim: Naturally occurring transmissible cancers have been identified in dogs.
source: Naturally occurring transmissible cancers have been identified in dogs (Murgia et al., 2006; Murchison et al., 2014; Baez-Ortega et al., 2019), Tasmanian devils (Murchison et al., 2012; Pye et al., 2016) and, more recently, in marine bivalves (Metzger et al., 2015; Metzger et al., 2016; Yonemitsu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Naturally occurring transmissible cancers have been identified in Tasmanian devils.
source: Naturally occurring transmissible cancers have been identified in dogs (Murgia et al., 2006; Murchison et al., 2014; Baez-Ortega et al., 2019), Tasmanian devils (Murchison et al., 2012; Pye et al., 2016) and, more recently, in marine bivalves (Metzger et al., 2015; Metzger et al., 2016; Yonemitsu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Naturally occurring transmissible cancers have been identified in marine bivalves.

evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Hemic neoplasia is a type of leukaemia cancer found in multiple species of bivalves, including oysters, mussels, cockles, and clams.
source: Hemic neoplasia (HN), also called disseminated neoplasia, is a type of leukaemia cancer found in multiple species of bivalves, including oysters, mussels, cockles, and clams (Carballal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about HN supported by a citation.

claim: Hemic neoplasia is also called disseminated neoplasia.
source: Hemic neoplasia (HN), also called disseminated neoplasia, is a type of leukaemia cancer found in multiple species of bivalves, including oysters, mussels, cockles, and clams (Carballal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a nomenclature statement supported by citation.

claim: Leukaemias in bivalves have been classically grouped under the same term because neoplastic cells share morphological features.
source: Although these leukaemias represent different diseases across bivalve species, they have been classically grouped under the same term because neoplastic cells share morphological features (Carballal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a historical statement about classification supported by citation.

claim: Some HNs have been proven to have a clonal transmissible behaviour.
source: Some HNs have been proven to have a clonal transmissible behaviour (Metzger et al., 2015), in which neoplastic cells, most likely haemocytes (i.e. the cells that populate the haemolymph and play a role in the immune response), are likely to be transmitted through marine water.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: Neoplastic cells in HN are most likely haemocytes.
source: Some HNs have been proven to have a clonal transmissible behaviour (Metzger et al., 2015), in which neoplastic cells, most likely haemocytes (i.e. the cells that populate the haemolymph and play a role in the immune response), are likely to be transmitted through marine water.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the nature of the cells involved.

claim: Haemocytes are the cells that populate the haemolymph and play a role in the immune response.
source: Some HNs have been proven to have a clonal transmissible behaviour (Metzger et al., 2015), in which neoplastic cells, most likely haemocytes (i.e. the cells that populate the haemolymph and play a role in the immune response), are likely to be transmitted through marine water.
evidence: This is a definitional statement based on established biological knowledge.

claim: Neoplastic cells in HN are likely to be transmitted through marine water.
source: Some HNs have been proven to have a clonal transmissible behaviour (Metzger et al., 2015), in which neoplastic cells, most likely haemocytes (i.e. the cells that populate the haemolymph and play a role in the immune response), are likely to be transmitted through marine water.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mode of transmission.

claim: In late stages of HN disease, leukaemic cells invade the surrounding tissues.
source: In late stages of the disease, leukaemic cells invade the surrounding tissues and, generally, animals die because of the infection (Carballal et al., 2015), although remissions have also been described (Burioli et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about disease progression supported by citation.

claim: Animals generally die because of HN infection.
source: In late stages of the disease, leukaemic cells invade the surrounding tissues and, generally, animals die because of the infection (Carballal et al., 2015), although remissions have also been described (Burioli et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about disease outcome supported by citation.

claim: Remissions of HN have been described.

claim: Leukaemic cells are typically transmitted between individuals from the same species.
source: Despite the observation that leukaemic cells are typically transmitted between individuals from the same species, on occasion they can infect and propagate across populations from a second, different bivalve species (Metzger et al., 2016; Yonemitsu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a general observation about transmission patterns supported by citations.

claim: Leukaemic cells can infect and propagate across populations from a second, different bivalve species.
source: Despite the observation that leukaemic cells are typically transmitted between individuals from the same species, on occasion they can infect and propagate across populations from a second, different bivalve species (Metzger et al., 2016; Yonemitsu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published research.

claim: These cancers represent a potential threat for the ecology of the marine environment.
source: Hence, these cancers represent a potential threat for the ecology of the marine environment, which argues for the necessity of their identification and characterization for their monitoring and prevention.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transmissible nature of the cancers.

claim: 345 clam specimens were collected from six sampling regions in the Atlantic and the Mediterranean coasts of Europe across five different countries.
source: We collected 345 clam specimens from six sampling regions in the Atlantic and the Mediterranean coasts of Europe across five different countries, including Spain, Portugal, France, Ireland, and Croatia (Figure 1a; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the sampling approach.

claim: The five countries sampled included Spain, Portugal, France, Ireland, and Croatia.
source: We collected 345 clam specimens from six sampling regions in the Atlantic and the Mediterranean coasts of Europe across five different countries, including Spain, Portugal, France, Ireland, and Croatia (Figure 1a; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a factual statement about sampling locations.

claim: Cytohistological examination identified HN-like tumours in eight specimens from two sampling points in Spain.
source: Cytohistological examination identified HN-like tumours in eight specimens from two sampling points in Spain (Figure 1b–e; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the diagnostic examination.

claim: Three HN-positive specimens were collected in Galicia, northwest of the Iberian Peninsula in the Atlantic Ocean.
source: Three HN-positive specimens (ERVV17-2995, ERVV17-2997, and ERVV17-3193) were collected in Galicia, northwest of the Iberian Peninsula in the Atlantic Ocean, and another five specimens (EMVV18-373, EMVV18-376, EMVV18-391, EMVV18-395, and EMVV18-400) were collected in the Balearic Islands, bathed by the Mediterranean Sea (Figure 1a; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a factual statement about sampling locations and results.

claim: Five HN-positive specimens were collected in the Balearic Islands, bathed by the Mediterranean Sea.
source: Three HN-positive specimens (ERVV17-2995, ERVV17-2997, and ERVV17-3193) were collected in Galicia, northwest of the Iberian Peninsula in the Atlantic Ocean, and another five specimens (EMVV18-373, EMVV18-376, EMVV18-391, EMVV18-395, and EMVV18-400) were collected in the Balearic Islands, bathed by the Mediterranean Sea (Figure 1a; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a factual statement about sampling locations and results.

claim: Four specimens showed a severe form of the disease classified as N3 stage.
source: Four of these specimens (ERVV17-2995, ERVV17-3193, EMVV18-391, and EMVV18-395) showed a severe form of the disease – classified as N3 stage – which is characterized by high levels of neoplastic cells infiltrating the gills, different levels of infiltration of the digestive gland and gonad, and low/very low infiltration of the mantle and foot (Figure 1d,e; Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a diagnostic finding based on histological examination.

claim: N3 stage is characterized by high levels of neoplastic cells infiltrating the gills, different levels of infiltration of the digestive gland and gonad, and low/very low infiltration of the mantle and foot.
source: Four of these specimens (ERVV17-2995, ERVV17-3193, EMVV18-391, and EMVV18-395) showed a severe form of the disease – classified as N3 stage – which is characterized by high levels of neoplastic cells infiltrating the gills, different levels of infiltration of the digestive gland and gonad, and low/very low infiltration of the mantle and foot (Figure 1d,e; Figure 1—figure supplement 1)

claim: One specimen was affected with an intermediate form of the disease classified as N2 stage.

claim: N2 stage is characterized by low levels of neoplastic cells infiltrating the gill vessels, digestive gland, and gonad, but not the foot.

claim: Three specimens were diagnosed with a light form of the disease classified as N1 stage.

claim: N1 stage is characterized by low levels of neoplastic cells infiltrating the gills vessels only, and no infiltration in the remaining tissues.

claim: Electron microscopy analysis revealed tumour cells with a round shape and a pleomorphic nucleus.
source: Electron microscopy analysis through gill's ultrathin sections from two neoplastic warty venus specimens (ERVV17-2995 and ERVV17-3193) revealed tumour cells with a round shape and a pleomorphic nucleus, which are morphological features that generally characterize bivalves' HN (Figure 1f; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from electron microscopy analysis, with visual evidence in figures.

claim: Round shape and pleomorphic nucleus are morphological features that generally characterize bivalves' HN.
source: Electron microscopy analysis through gill's ultrathin sections from two neoplastic warty venus specimens (ERVV17-2995 and ERVV17-3193) revealed tumour cells with a round shape and a pleomorphic nucleus, which are morphological features that generally characterize bivalves' HN (Figure 1f; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a statement about general characteristics of HN based on established knowledge.

claim: V. verrucosa typically shows a 2n = 38 karyotype with metacentric chromosomes that are homogeneous in size.
source: Although the species typically shows a 2n = 38 karyotype with metacentric chromosomes that are homogeneous in size (García-Souto et al., 2015), the tumoural metaphases from this individual showed around 100 chromosomes that were variable in size and shape (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is a statement about normal karyotype supported by citation.

claim: The tumoural metaphases from specimen EVVV11-02 showed around 100 chromosomes that were variable in size and shape.
source: Although the species typically shows a 2n = 38 karyotype with metacentric chromosomes that are homogeneous in size (García-Souto et al., 2015), the tumoural metaphases from this individual showed around 100 chromosomes that were variable in size and shape (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is a cytogenetic finding from the analysis of metaphase chromosomes.

claim: Whole-genome sequencing was carried out with Illumina paired-ends in DNA samples isolated from the tumoural haemolymph from eight out of nine neoplastic specimens.
source: To obtain some biological insights into the clonal dynamics of this cancer, we carried out whole-genome sequencing with Illumina paired-ends in DNA samples isolated from the tumoural haemolymph from eight out of nine neoplastic specimens mentioned above (Table 1).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the sequencing approach.

claim: Foot typically represents the tissue with lower infiltration of neoplastic cells.
source: Their feet were also sequenced, as foot typically represents the tissue with lower infiltration of neoplastic cells, making it a good candidate tissue to act as 'matched-normal' (i.e. host tissue).
evidence: This is an observation about tissue infiltration patterns in HN.

claim: In six out of eight sequenced neoplastic specimens, the results revealed an overrepresentation (>99%) of reads mapping to Cox1 DNA sequences that exclusively identified two different clam species.
source: In six out of eight sequenced neoplastic specimens, the results revealed an overrepresentation (>99%) of reads in the sequenced tissues mapping to Cox1 DNA sequences that exclusively identified two different clam species (Figure 2a): the expected one, warty venus clam (V. verrucosa), and a second, unexpected one, the striped venus (C. gallina), a clam that inhabits the Mediterranean Sea (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the sequencing data analysis.

claim: The two clam species identified were warty venus clam (V. verrucosa) and striped venus (C. gallina).
source: In six out of eight sequenced neoplastic specimens, the results revealed an overrepresentation (>99%) of reads in the sequenced tissues mapping to Cox1 DNA sequences that exclusively identified two different clam species (Figure 2a): the expected one, warty venus clam (V. verrucosa), and a second, unexpected one, the striped venus (C. gallina), a clam that inhabits the Mediterranean Sea (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a finding from the Cox1 mapping analysis.

claim: C. gallina is a clam that inhabits the Mediterranean Sea.

claim: PCR and capillary sequencing of Cox1 in the haemolymph of two neoplastic specimens revealed an electropherogram with overlapping peaks apparently containing two different haplotypes.
source: Preliminary analysis by PCR and capillary sequencing of Cox1 in the haemolymph of two neoplastic specimens, EMVV18-373 and EVVV11-02, revealed an electropherogram with overlapping peaks apparently containing two different haplotypes that match the reference Cox1 sequences for warty and striped venus (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a finding from PCR and capillary sequencing analysis.

claim: The two haplotypes match the reference Cox1 sequences for warty and striped venus.

evidence: This is a finding from sequence comparison analysis.

claim: The comparative analysis of the nucleotide sequences from both mitogenomes confirms that both species are relatively close within the subfamily Venerinae.
source: The comparative analysis of the nucleotide sequences from both mitogenomes confirms that, although both species are relatively close within the subfamily Venerinae (Canapa et al., 1996), they represent distinct sister species, showing a Kimura's two-parameter nucleotide distance (K2P) equal to 21.13%.
evidence: This is a finding from comparative genomic analysis, supported by citation.

claim: V. verrucosa and C. gallina represent distinct sister species.
source: The comparative analysis of the nucleotide sequences from both mitogenomes confirms that, although both species are relatively close within the subfamily Venerinae (Canapa et al., 1996), they represent distinct sister species, showing a Kimura's two-parameter nucleotide distance (K2P) equal to 21.13%.
evidence: This is a finding from comparative genomic analysis.

claim: V. verrucosa and C. gallina show a Kimura's two-parameter nucleotide distance (K2P) equal to 21.13%.
source: The comparative analysis of the nucleotide sequences from both mitogenomes confirms that, although both species are relatively close within the subfamily Venerinae (Canapa et al., 1996), they represent distinct sister species, showing a Kimura's two-parameter nucleotide distance (K2P) equal to 21.13%.

claim: Mapping of paired-end sequencing data confirmed the coexistence of two different mtDNA haplotypes in the six examined neoplastic samples.
source: Then, we mapped the paired-end sequencing data from the six neoplastic specimens with evidence of interspecies cancer transmission onto the two reconstructed species-specific mtDNA genomes. This approach confirmed the coexistence of two different mtDNA haplotypes in the six examined neoplastic samples, matching the canonical mtDNA genomes from the two clam species.
evidence: This is a finding from mapping analysis of sequencing data.

claim: The two mtDNA haplotypes match the canonical mtDNA genomes from the two clam species.

This approach confirmed the coexistence of two different mtDNA haplotypes in the six examined neoplastic samples, matching the canonical mtDNA genomes from the two clam species.

claim: In specimen EMVV18-400, the striped venus mtDNA is the most abundant in the haemolymph.
source: For example, in a N2-stage specimen (EMVV18-400), this analysis revealed different proportion of tumour and host mtDNA molecules in the two tissue types sequenced (Figure 2d). Here, the striped venus mtDNA results the most abundant in the haemolymph, in which tumour cells are dominant over the remaining cell types, and the lower in the matched-normal tissue (i.e. infiltrated foot), where tumour cells represent a minor fraction of the total.
evidence: This is a finding from mtDNA read depth analysis.

Here, the striped venus mtDNA results the most abundant in the haemolymph, in which tumour cells are dominant over the remaining cell types, and the lower in the matched-normal tissue (i.e. infiltrated foot), where tumour cells represent a minor fraction of the total.

claim: Phylogenetic analysis shows that tumour and non-tumour sequences from neoplastic warty venus specimens define two well-differentiated clades.
source: The results show that tumour and non-tumour sequences from neoplastic warty venus specimens define two well-differentiated clades, and that tumoural warty venus sequences are all identical and closer to striped venus mtDNA than to its own (warty venus) (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Tumoural warty venus sequences are all identical.
source: The results show that tumour and non-tumour sequences from neoplastic warty venus specimens define two well-differentiated clades, and that tumoural warty venus sequences are all identical and closer to striped venus mtDNA than to its own (warty venus) (Figure 2e).

claim: Tumoural warty venus sequences are closer to striped venus mtDNA than to warty venus mtDNA.

claim: The data support the existence of a single cancer clone originated in the striped venus clam C. gallina that was transmitted to V. verrucosa.
source: Overall, these data support the existence of a single cancer clone originated in the striped venus clam C. gallina that was transmitted to V. verrucosa.

claim: Transmissible cancers are known to occasionally acquire mitochondria from transient hosts.
source: Transmissible cancers are known to occasionally acquire mitochondria from transient hosts (Strakova et al., 2016; Strakova et al., 2020), which can lead to misinterpretation of their evolutionary history.
evidence: This is a statement about transmissible cancer biology supported by citations.

claim: Acquisition of mitochondria from transient hosts can lead to misinterpretation of transmissible cancer evolutionary history.
source: Transmissible cancers are known to occasionally acquire mitochondria from transient hosts (Strakova et al., 2016; Strakova et al., 2020), which can lead to misinterpretation of their evolutionary history.

claim: Two confident candidate genomic regions were identified: a 2.9-kb long region from DEAH12 and a 2.2-kb long fragment from TFIIH.
source: Thus, we looked for nuclear markers to confirm the striped venus origin of this cancer lineage. We performed a preliminary draft assembly of the warty venus and the striped venus nuclear 'reference' genomes, using the paired-end sequencing data from two non-neoplastic animals. Then, we used bioinformatic approaches to find single copy nuclear genes that were homologous between the two species, identifying two confident candidate genomic regions (see Methods): a 2.9-kb long region from DEAH12, a gene that encodes for an ATP-dependent RNA helicase, and a 2.2-kb long fragment from the Transcription Factor II Human-like gene, TFIIH.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the identification of nuclear markers.

claim: DEAH12 encodes for an ATP-dependent RNA helicase.
source: Thus, we looked for nuclear markers to confirm the striped venus origin of this cancer lineage. We performed a preliminary draft assembly of the warty venus and the striped venus nuclear 'reference' genomes, using the paired-end sequencing data from two non-neoplastic animals. Then, we used bioinformatic approaches to find single copy nuclear genes that were homologous between the two species, identifying two confident candidate genomic regions (see Methods): a 2.9-kb long region from DEAH12, a gene that encodes for an ATP-dependent RNA helicase, and a 2.2-kb long fragment from the Transcription Factor II Human-like gene, TFIIH.
evidence: This is a statement about gene function based on established knowledge.

claim: PCR amplification and capillary sequencing provided 14 sites for the DEAH12 locus with fixed SNVs (allele frequency >95%).
source: With the idea of finding differentially fixed single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) between both species, we performed PCR amplification and capillary sequencing on a 441 bp fragment from the DEAH12, and a 559 bp fragment from TFIIH, in 2 cohorts of non-neoplastic warty venus specimens (12 for DEAH12 and 15 for TFIIH), 2 cohorts of non-neoplastic striped venus (9 for DEAH12 and 12 for TFIIH), and 1 specimen of its sister species C. striatula. This analysis provided 14 and 15 sites, respectively, for the DEAH12 and the TFIIH loci, with fixed SNVs (allele frequency >95%) that allowed to discriminate between the 3 relevant species and the tumour (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a finding from PCR and sequencing analysis.

evidence: This is a finding from PCR and sequencing analysis.

claim: The fixed SNVs allowed to discriminate between the 3 relevant species and the tumour.
source: With the idea of finding differentially fixed single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) between both species, we performed PCR amplification and capillary sequencing on a 441 bp fragment from the DEAH12, and a 559 bp fragment from TFIIH, in 2 cohorts of non-neoplastic warty venus specimens (12 for DEAH12 and 15 for TFIIH), 2 cohorts of non-neoplastic striped venus (9 for DEAH12 and 12 for TFIIH), and 1 specimen of its sister species C. striatula. This analysis provided 14 and 15 sites, respectively, for the DEAH12 and the TFIIH loci, with fixed SNVs (allele frequency >95%) that allowed to discriminate between the 3 relevant species and the tumour (Figure 3a).

claim: The phylogeny for the DEAH12 locus confirmed both the monophyly of the tumoural sequences and their closer relationship to C. gallina than to the host species.
source: On the one hand, the phylogeny for the DEAH12 locus confirmed both the monophyly of the tumoural sequences and their closer relationship to C. gallina than to the host species (Figure 3b), which were also observed in the mtDNA analysis.
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic analysis of nuclear markers.

claim: The phylogeny derived from the TFIIH locus showed that the tumours remained monophyletic but were positioned in a basal branch relative to C. gallina and V. verrucosa.
source: However, the phylogeny derived from the TFIIH locus showed that, although the tumours remained monophyletic, they were positioned in a basal branch relative to C. gallina and V. verrucosa (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic analysis of nuclear markers.

claim: The multilocus species tree confirmed that warty venus tumours are closer to striped venus specimens than to non-neoplastic warty venus sequences from the same diseased specimens.
source: Hence, to resolve these differences we also obtained a multilocus species tree based on the alignment of both the mtDNA and the two nuclear genes. This new phylogeny confirmed that warty venus tumours are closer to striped venus specimens than to non-neoplastic warty venus sequences from the same diseased specimens, while the non-neoplastic sequences conformed a more distant warty venus lineage (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a finding from multilocus phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The non-neoplastic sequences conformed a more distant warty venus lineage.
source: Hence, to resolve these differences we also obtained a multilocus species tree based on the alignment of both the mtDNA and the two nuclear genes. This new phylogeny confirmed that warty venus tumours are closer to striped venus specimens than to non-neoplastic warty venus sequences from the same diseased specimens, while the non-neoplastic sequences conformed a more distant warty venus lineage (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a finding from multilocus phylogenetic analysis.

claim: FISH revealed that CL4 and CL17 repeats are very abundant in heterochromatic regions from the genomes of the canonical striped venus and the neoplastic warty venus specimens tested.
source: This FISH approach revealed that the mentioned repeats are very abundant in heterochromatic regions from the genomes of the canonical striped venus and the neoplastic warty venus specimens tested (Figure 3d; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from FISH analysis.

claim: CL4 and CL17 repeats were absent in the metaphases from all the healthy warty venus individuals.
source: However, the repeats were absent in the metaphases from all the healthy warty venus individuals (Figure 3d; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from FISH analysis.

claim: The chromosomes with CL4 and CL17 satellites found in neoplastic warty venus specimens derive from C. gallina.
source: These results suggest that the relevant chromosomes with CL4 and CL17 satellites found in neoplastic warty venus specimens derive from C. gallina, supporting that a tumour originated in C. gallina was transmitted to V. verrucosa.
evidence: This is an inference from the FISH analysis results.

claim: A screening for HN was performed in natural populations of striped venus clams from the species C. gallina (n = 213) and C. striatula (n = 9) at five additional sampling points across two countries.
source: To find out whether this cancer is present in the clam species where it first arose, we performed a screening for its presence in natural populations of striped venus clams from the species C. gallina (n = 213) and C. striatula (n = 9) at five additional sampling points across two countries (Supplementary file 1), including Spain (n = 115) and Italy (n = 107).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the screening approach.

claim: Histological analyses did not show any traces of HN in striped venus specimens.
source: Histological analyses did not show any traces of HN in these specimens.
evidence: This is a finding from histological examination.

claim: The virtual absence of this tumour in natural populations of striped venus clams may suggest that today this leukaemia is being mainly, if not exclusively, transmitted between specimens of the recipient species, warty venus.
source: The virtual absence of this tumour in natural populations of striped venus clams may suggest that today this leukaemia is being mainly, if not exclusively, transmitted between specimens of the recipient species, warty venus.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the screening results.

claim: This transmissible leukaemia was identified in warty venus clams from two sampling points that are more than 1000 nautical miles away in the coasts of Spain, bathed by two different seas, the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea.
source: Overall, the results provided here reveal the existence of a transmissible leukaemia originated in a striped venus clam, most likely C. gallina, which was transmitted to a second species, the warty venus clam (V. verrucosa), and among whose specimens it currently propagates. We identified this parasitic cancer in warty venus clams from two sampling points that are more than 1000 nautical miles away in the coasts of Spain, bathed by two different seas, the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the geographic distribution findings.

claim: The analysis of mitochondrial and nuclear gene sequences revealed no nucleotide diversity within the seven tumours sequenced.
source: The analysis of mitochondrial and nuclear gene sequences revealed no nucleotide diversity within the seven tumours sequenced, which supports that all belong to the same neoplastic lineage that spreads between Veneridae clams in the Seas of Southern Europe.
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis.

claim: The lack of genetic variation supports that all tumours belong to the same neoplastic lineage that spreads between Veneridae clams in the Seas of Southern Europe.
source: The analysis of mitochondrial and nuclear gene sequences revealed no nucleotide diversity within the seven tumours sequenced, which supports that all belong to the same neoplastic lineage that spreads between Veneridae clams in the Seas of Southern Europe.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of genetic variation observed.

claim: This cancer arose before 2011, when the neoplastic warty venus specimen EVVV11-02 was collected.
source: Although we ignore the age of this cancer clone, we can confirm it arose before 2011, when the neoplastic warty venus specimen EVVV11-02 was collected.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the collection date of a neoplastic specimen.

claim: The apparent lack of genetic variation between all tumours suggests either that this cancer is very recent, or that it may have been unintentionally scattered by the action of man.
source: The apparent lack of genetic variation between all tumours, even from distant sampling points, suggests either that this cancer is very recent, or that it may have been unintentionally scattered by the action of man, a way of transmission that has been proposed for other bivalve transmissible cancers (Yonemitsu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the genetic data, with citation support for human-mediated transmission.

claim: Human-mediated transmission has been proposed for other bivalve transmissible cancers.
source: The apparent lack of genetic variation between all tumours, even from distant sampling points, suggests either that this cancer is very recent, or that it may have been unintentionally scattered by the action of man, a way of transmission that has been proposed for other bivalve transmissible cancers (Yonemitsu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claim: The mitochondrial genome of V. verrucosa is 18,092 bp long.
source: These reconstructions resulted in 18,092- and 17,618-bp long mtDNA genomes for the warty venus and the striped venus clam, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from genome assembly.

claim: The mitochondrial genome of C. gallina is 17,618 bp long.
source: These reconstructions resulted in 18,092- and 17,618-bp long mtDNA genomes for the warty venus and the striped venus clam, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from genome assembly.

claim: CL4 is a satellite DNA repeat of 332-bp long monomers.
source: We focused on two satellite DNA repeats, namely CL4 and CL17. The satellites represent repeats of 332- and 429-bp long monomers, respectively, and were identified in a preliminary bioinformatics screening of the striped venus reference genome (see methods).
evidence: This is a finding from bioinformatic analysis.

claim: CL17 is a satellite DNA repeat of 429-bp long monomers.
source: We focused on two satellite DNA repeats, namely CL4 and CL17. The satellites represent repeats of 332- and 429-bp long monomers, respectively, and were identified in a preliminary bioinformatics screening of the striped venus reference genome (see methods).
evidence: This is a finding from bioinformatic analysis.
